pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis refines the previous approach by coupling ion implantation with pre‐experimental simulation to optimize the diffusion and replenishment of Y, ensuring that a self‐healing Y2O3 tribofilm is maintained throughout variable thermal and load conditions.

fields.hypothesis: Optimized surface yttrium ion implantation with pre‐validated diffusion kinetics will enable sustained in situ formation of a lubricious Y2O3 tribofilm on CoCrFeNi under sliding from room temperature to 800 °C.
fields.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy produced by conventional melting, featuring a homogeneous single‐phase microstructure with no intentional surface modification.
fields.intervention: Perform a shallow yttrium ion implantation on the alloy surface with a calibrated dose (targeting ~1–2 at% Y within the top few hundred nanometers), where the dose and depth are pre‐optimized via thermal/diffusion simulations to ensure an adequate Y reservoir throughout sliding wear.
fields.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests conducted in ambient atmosphere over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, under a series of loads and sliding speeds representative of variable service conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: The implantation generates a Y‐rich near-surface region that, during sliding-induced local heating, oxidizes to form a fine, continuous Y2O3 nanolayer while the bulk microstructure remains intact.
fields.mechanism: Under low temperatures the effect is minimal, but as the interface temperature rises during sliding (especially above ~400 °C), implanted Y diffuses and readily reacts with oxygen to in situ build a stable Y2O3 tribofilm. This film minimizes direct metal–metal contact by reducing asperity interaction, thus lowering friction and wear. Validation of the proper Y reservoir via simulation addresses concerns that excessive depletion or embrittlement might occur.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to unimplanted samples, the Y-implanted specimens should show a consistently lower friction coefficient (modest benefit at room temperature and increasingly pronounced reduction above ~400 °C) and reduced wear rate over the entire temperature range.
fields.baseline: CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy with no yttrium implantation.
fields.boundary: The improvement depends on optimized ion dose/depth; if the implanted Y is insufficient (or if excessive, causing embrittlement), the continuous tribofilm may not form reliably. Also, the kinetics of oxide formation must match the sliding-induced thermal cycles.
fields.uncertainty: While oxide tribofilms have demonstrated lubrication in related systems (TXT::wikipedia::Wear::011, TXT::doitpoms::tribology/printall::039), the exact quantitative friction and wear reduction achievable here remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one with the optimized yttrium ion implantation (with dose validated by pre-tests/simulations) and one unmodified. Subject both sets to identical dry sliding tests from room temperature to 800 °C while varying load and sliding speed.
measurements: Measure coefficient of friction and wear rate as a function of temperature.
Conduct surface analyses (SEM/EDS, XRD) to assess the presence, continuity, and morphology of the Y2O3 tribofilm.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-implanted samples do not yield a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear across the entire temperature range or if a continuous Y2O3 layer is not observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C12
pool.builds_on: the observation that introducing reinforcing phases in surface composites (as in HEA-reinforced systems) can modify wear behavior, now adapted to CoCrFeNi through in situ carbide formation combined with carbon-induced lubrication.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a laser surface carburization route for CoCrFeNi to trigger tailored, in situ precipitation of carbide phases along with carbon segregation to form a self-lubricating tribofilm—a strategy that has not been reported in the referenced work.

fields.hypothesis: Employ laser surface carburization on CoCrFeNi to induce in situ formation of nanoscale chromium carbide precipitates that promote the generation of a self‐lubricating, carbon‐rich tribofilm during sliding over a wide temperature range.
fields.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous single-phase FCC solid solution and its conventional native surface oxide.
fields.intervention: Apply a laser surface carburization treatment that locally enriches the surface with carbon (to a depth of a few microns) under controlled thermal gradients, encouraging the formation of nanostructured chromium carbides within a carbon-enriched surface layer.
fields.conditions: Pin-on-disc sliding tests conducted in ambient air from room temperature up to 800 °C under varying loads and sliding speeds.
fields.structural_mediator: A refined surface layer with uniformly dispersed, nanoscale Cr-rich carbide precipitates embedded in a carbon-saturated CoCrFeNi matrix.
fields.mechanism: Under sliding conditions, the in situ generated carbide phase increases hardness and load-bearing capacity, while the surface-enriched carbon partially segregates to form graphitic-like phases. This graphitic tribofilm reduces interfacial shear by providing a low-shear, self-lubricating barrier that minimizes adhesive wear. Such a dual mechanism addresses both friction and wear over a broad temperature range.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to unmodified CoCrFeNi, the laser carburized samples are expected to display a significantly lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate across the full temperature range, with post-test analysis revealing both carbide precipitates and evidence of a carbon-rich tribofilm on the worn surfaces.
fields.baseline: Standard CoCrFeNi alloy that forms non-uniform native oxides and lacks the in situ reinforcement and self-lubricating phases, resulting in higher friction and wear, especially at elevated temperatures.
fields.boundary: Effectiveness is anticipated from room temperature to ~800 °C under moderate to high loads; however, extremely oxidizing conditions or temperatures inducing excessive oxidation of the graphitic phase might compromise performance.
fields.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of carbon segregation to form a lubricious film and the stability of the carbide phase during cyclic sliding remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one group subjected to laser surface carburization and a control group with no treatment. Conduct pin-on-disc wear tests from room temperature to 800 °C under identical load and speed conditions. Afterwards, use Raman spectroscopy, XRD, and SEM/EDS analyses to check for the presence of carbides and graphitic phases in the worn surfaces.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature
Wear rate (mass loss) under specified loads
Identification and distribution of carbide and carbon-rich (graphitic) phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carburized samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear rates compared to untreated samples, or if no evidence of carbide precipitates and graphitic tribofilm is found on the worn surfaces, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C6
top3.builds_on: the reactive wear protection strategy in the paper (PMC8448869::web::017::discussion) by tailoring the surface oxidation reaction to form a ductile, well-adhered oxide layer, leveraging yttrium’s known effect on oxide scale adhesion.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a surface modification via yttrium ion implantation—a single, surface-targeted intervention that does not alter the bulk composition of the CoCrFeNi alloy—to catalyze the formation of a beneficial, Y-rich oxide nanocomposite layer for improved tribological performance over a wide temperature range.

fields.hypothesis: Introduce a surface-specific modification by implanting a thin layer of yttrium (Y) into the top few tens of nanometers of the CoCrFeNi alloy to catalyze the formation of an adherent, ductile, Y-rich oxide phase that enhances tribological performance over 0–800 °C.
fields.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a pristine, homogeneous surface that oxidizes uncontrollably during sliding, producing non-uniform oxide scales with high friction and accelerated wear.
fields.intervention: Perform a surface yttrium ion implantation treatment (e.g., at sub-1 at.% overall Y concentration confined to the top 50–100 nm) without altering the bulk alloy composition.
fields.conditions: Dry ball‐on‐disk sliding tests in ambient air carried out over the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under moderate-to-high contact loads.
fields.structural_mediator: Yttrium, due to its high oxygen affinity, promotes the nucleation of a Y-rich oxide during initial oxidation. The resulting ultrathin Y-enriched oxide phase is expected to be highly adherent and to form a coherent, nanocomposite interface (with Y-rich oxide islands dispersed within a mixed oxide matrix) that improves lubrication.
fields.mechanism: Yttrium’s known ability to improve oxide adhesion (as observed in superalloy applications) leads to a stable, well-adhered, and uniform oxide scale. The presence of the Y-rich oxide phase can interrupt the growth of continuous, brittle oxides and foster a ductile, homogeneous nanostructure at the sliding interface. This engineered surface facilitates low shear during sliding and resists crack initiation, thereby reducing friction and wear.
fields.predicted_outcome: A steady-state friction coefficient approaching ~0.1 and a wear rate reduced by roughly one order of magnitude relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi, sustained from room temperature up to 800 °C.
fields.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi, which readily forms non-uniform oxide layers with higher friction (~0.25) and greater wear volumes.
fields.boundary: The success of this intervention depends on finely controlling the Y dose and implantation depth; excessive Y could lead to thick or brittle oxide scales, while insufficient Y may not effectively catalyze the desired oxide phase. The thermal stability of the Y-rich oxide phase under cyclic temperature and load variations is also critical.
fields.uncertainty: Although yttrium's oxide adhesion benefits are well-documented in other systems, its impact on the tribological performance of a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy over a wide temperature range requires experimental validation, and quantitative effects remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of specimens: one set of CoCrFeNi treated with a controlled yttrium ion implantation (targeting <1 at.% Y in the top ~50–100 nm) and one untreated control. Subject both groups to identical dry ball‐on‐disk sliding tests in ambient air over 0–800 °C.
measurements: Continuously record the friction coefficient during sliding cycles.
Quantify wear track volumes using 3D optical profilometry.
Conduct surface and cross-sectional analysis by TEM, EDS, and XPS to detect the formation, continuity, and phase of the Y-rich oxide.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-implanted specimens do not exhibit a significant reduction in friction (target ~0.1) and a roughly tenfold lower wear rate compared to controls, or if a well-adhered Y-rich oxide phase is not present at the surface, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C11
top3.builds_on: The original idea of using yttrium ion implantation to form lubricious Y2O3 (as proposed in the earlier paper-based hypothesis) with the improvement of incorporating pre-validating diffusion kinetics to ensure a sustained Y reservoir.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis refines the previous approach by coupling ion implantation with pre‐experimental simulation to optimize the diffusion and replenishment of Y, ensuring that a self‐healing Y2O3 tribofilm is maintained throughout variable thermal and load conditions.

fields.hypothesis: Optimized surface yttrium ion implantation with pre‐validated diffusion kinetics will enable sustained in situ formation of a lubricious Y2O3 tribofilm on CoCrFeNi under sliding from room temperature to 800 °C.
fields.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy produced by conventional melting, featuring a homogeneous single‐phase microstructure with no intentional surface modification.
fields.intervention: Perform a shallow yttrium ion implantation on the alloy surface with a calibrated dose (targeting ~1–2 at% Y within the top few hundred nanometers), where the dose and depth are pre‐optimized via thermal/diffusion simulations to ensure an adequate Y reservoir throughout sliding wear.
fields.conditions: Dry sliding wear tests conducted in ambient atmosphere over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, under a series of loads and sliding speeds representative of variable service conditions.
fields.structural_mediator: The implantation generates a Y‐rich near-surface region that, during sliding-induced local heating, oxidizes to form a fine, continuous Y2O3 nanolayer while the bulk microstructure remains intact.
fields.mechanism: Under low temperatures the effect is minimal, but as the interface temperature rises during sliding (especially above ~400 °C), implanted Y diffuses and readily reacts with oxygen to in situ build a stable Y2O3 tribofilm. This film minimizes direct metal–metal contact by reducing asperity interaction, thus lowering friction and wear. Validation of the proper Y reservoir via simulation addresses concerns that excessive depletion or embrittlement might occur.
fields.predicted_outcome: Relative to unimplanted samples, the Y-implanted specimens should show a consistently lower friction coefficient (modest benefit at room temperature and increasingly pronounced reduction above ~400 °C) and reduced wear rate over the entire temperature range.
fields.baseline: CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy with no yttrium implantation.
fields.boundary: The improvement depends on optimized ion dose/depth; if the implanted Y is insufficient (or if excessive, causing embrittlement), the continuous tribofilm may not form reliably. Also, the kinetics of oxide formation must match the sliding-induced thermal cycles.
fields.uncertainty: While oxide tribofilms have demonstrated lubrication in related systems (TXT::wikipedia::Wear::011, TXT::doitpoms::tribology/printall::039), the exact quantitative friction and wear reduction achievable here remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one with the optimized yttrium ion implantation (with dose validated by pre-tests/simulations) and one unmodified. Subject both sets to identical dry sliding tests from room temperature to 800 °C while varying load and sliding speed.
measurements: Measure coefficient of friction and wear rate as a function of temperature.
Conduct surface analyses (SEM/EDS, XRD) to assess the presence, continuity, and morphology of the Y2O3 tribofilm.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-implanted samples do not yield a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear across the entire temperature range or if a continuous Y2O3 layer is not observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C5
top3.builds_on: the reactive wear protection concept from the paper (PMC8448869::web::017::discussion) by promoting a controlled in-situ oxide nanocomposite formation, and extends it by employing a microalloying element known to form lubricious oxide phases under high-temperature conditions.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes the use of boron addition in the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy—a new strategy not explored in the paper—to tailor the oxidation pathway so that a ductile, self-lubricating borate-rich amorphous nanocomposite surface forms during sliding.

fields.hypothesis: Add a minor boron (B) microalloying addition (e.g., 2 at.%) to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy to promote the in-situ formation of a lubricious, borate-rich amorphous oxide nanocomposite during sliding.
fields.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with homogeneous composition that, when sliding, forms uncontrolled or non-optimized oxide scales with high friction and wear.
fields.intervention: Introduce ~2 at.% boron during alloy synthesis (e.g., via arc melting or sputtering) so that B is distributed in the matrix.
fields.conditions: Dry ball‐on‐disk sliding tests in ambient air over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under moderate-to-high contact loads.
fields.structural_mediator: During sliding at varying temperatures, B is expected to segregate at the surface and react with available oxygen to form a thin (200–400 nm) borate-rich amorphous oxide layer possibly intermixed with other oxides; this nanocomposite feature should be continuous and well adhered.
fields.mechanism: Boron oxide (B2O3) has a low glass transition temperature and a relatively low shear strength compared to conventional silicates. Its presence in an amorphous nanocomposite can enable viscous, self-healing, and ductile oxide behavior. This lubricious phase reduces shear resistance at the sliding interface and accommodates plastic strain homogeneously, thus mitigating friction and wear over the full temperature span.
fields.predicted_outcome: A steady-state friction coefficient near ~0.1 and a wear rate reduced by roughly one order of magnitude relative to the untreated CoCrFeNi, maintained from room temperature to 800 °C.
fields.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi, which typically develops less-controlled oxide scales with friction around ~0.25 and higher wear volumes.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect relies on precise B content; too high a concentration could embrittle the bulk or lead to excessive oxide formation, and the mechanism must be robust even under rapid temperature transients and varying loads.
fields.uncertainty: While borate glasses are known for their lubricious behavior at high temperatures, the exact extent of ductility and self-healing in a CoCrFeNi matrix with 2 at.% B over 0–800 °C remains to be quantitatively determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one set of CoCrFeNi with ~2 at.% B addition and a control set without B. Subject both sets to identical dry ball‐on‐disk sliding tests in ambient air covering temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C.
measurements: Continuously record the steady-state friction coefficient.
Quantify wear track volumes using 3D optical profilometry.
Characterize the near-surface using TEM/EDS/XPS to verify formation, thickness, and amorphous nature of a borate-rich oxide nanocomposite.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the B-doped specimens do not exhibit a friction coefficient near ~0.1 and a reduction in wear rate by roughly 10× compared to the control, or if a continuous, ductile borate-rich amorphous oxide layer is absent, then the hypothesis is falsified.
